title: Teach Students to Memorize Sets of Knowns
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. introduces the concept of 'sets of knowns' — foundational disciplinary knowledge that students should commit to memory — drawing on Montana educator Tammy Elser's Indian Education work to illustrate how ignorance of foundational knowledge forecloses sophisticated thought. He argues that teachers across all content areas should identify their discipline's core memorizable knowledge and guide students to build it systematically, offering his world history date-memorization practice as a detailed case study. The article includes an eight-step classroom protocol for introducing memorization to skeptical students — using spaced retrieval across four lists within a single class period — that produces rapid, measurable growth and converts skeptics in a single fifteen-minute activity. Stuart Jr. then connects this practice to all five key beliefs simultaneously: Credibility (the teacher demonstrates they can teach hard things quickly), Value (the student begins to see why foundational knowledge matters), Effort and Efficacy (success is immediate and visible), and Belonging (students reframe their identity as people who can memorize). He closes with the essential caveat that memorization only sticks when the knowledge is embedded in meaningful, recurring practice throughout the year.
points: Identify foundational 'sets of knowns' for your discipline — dates, formulas, shortcuts, essential vocabulary — as the prerequisite knowledge that makes higher-order thinking in your field possible rather than accidental.

The eight-step copy-cover-recall-compare-rescore-repeat protocol teaches students to memorize through distributed practice within a single fifteen-minute activity, demonstrating to skeptics that memorization is teachable, not just innate.

Pre- and post-activity writing prompts ('Are you the kind of person who can memorize dates?') frame the exercise as a Belonging and Efficacy cultivation moment, helping students revise their self-concept as learners.

A single well-run memorization activity builds all five key beliefs simultaneously: Credibility (you teach, not just exhort), Value (you argue why it matters), Effort (applied effort yields quick gains), Efficacy (success is engineered in), and Belonging (students see themselves as capable).

Memorized knowledge must be embedded in meaningful, recurring practice — readings, writings, and discussions that use the knowledge — or it will not stick; isolated memorization exercises do not produce durable learning.
quotes: How do we expect them to create complex thoughts, experience intellectual breakthroughs, or even gain basic comprehension of course concepts if we've not gifted them with a chance to commit foundational knowledge to memory?
It doesn't matter that there's Google — I want it in their brains, and I want to show them that there's a lot of unadvertised joy in this old-fashioned idea of building knowledge.
The kids now know that I'm a teacher who can help them do things they didn't think they could do, and I can do it fairly quickly. I do more than say, "Work harder, punk." I teach them.
Memorizing sets of knowns is really only effective (and is so much easier) when the knowledge is meaningful. If your sets of knowns aren't marinated in meaningful practice, then they won't stick.
By limiting the list to five dates and explicitly guiding them in the memorization process, I'm proving that success is possible.
Especially with the opening and closing writing exercises, I'm helping my kids to see themselves as the kinds of people who can do the work I'll ask them to do.
